quote: Be regular and orderly in your life, like a bourgeois, so that you may be violent and original in your work.
source: Gustave Flaubert, Correspondance, vol. IV, p. 280, letter to Madame Tennant, Jour de Noël 1876

evidence.where: Second re-verification. I took up the two rescue candidates the refutation named and tested them through Open Library's search inside, which does index the lending copies of Steegmuller's letters volumes (it returned The letters of Gustave Flaubert, 1857-1880 on an unrelated query, so its text is in the index). Exact phrase searches for every circulating rendering returned no volume of Flaubert's letters in English: not Steegmuller's Selected Letters of 1953, not the Harvard two volumes of 1980 and 1982, not Rumbold 1951. What the searches did return is five different English sentences in secondary books: Be regular and orderly in your life like a bourgeois, so that you may be violent and original in your work (Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, Austin Kleon, Peter Bollen, David Kirby and many more); Be regular and ordinary in your life, like a bourgeois, so that you can be violent and original in your works (Elizabeth Taylor's A Wreath of Roses 1949, Kennedy Fraser, John Walker's National Gallery of Art volumes, Philip Hook); Be regular and ordinary in your life like a bourgeois, in order to be violent and original in your works (James C. Sanford, Great Freethinkers, which also renders the opening as a principle of aesthetics, a rule for artists); the orderly and ordinary hybrids; and Be steady and well ordered in your life so that you can be fierce and original in your work (David Allen and a shelf of productivity books). The only Steegmuller text that prints any of it is his biography Flaubert and Madame Bovary: A Double Portrait, where six scanned editions all show the same fragment, his own prose running into an opening quotation mark: for artists, “so that you can be violent and original in your works. Shifted phrase searches place Steegmuller outside the wording like a bourgeois, so that you can be violent and original in your works, so what he encloses in quotation marks begins at so that and the first half of the sentence is not his quoted English. The French remains sound and is not in question: Correspondance tome IV, page 280, scan correspondance04flauuoft, the letter headed A Madame Tennant, Jour de Noël 1876, reading Soyez réglé dans votre vie et ordinaire comme un bourgeois, afin d'être violent et original dans vos oeuvres. Google Books is hard quota blocked at zero queries per day, the archive.org search inside endpoints on the lending volumes return Item not available, and the WebSearch budget for the session was spent, so Open Library's index was the instrument.
evidence.edition: Gustave Flaubert, Correspondance, tome IV (Charpentier), p. 280; Francis Steegmuller, Flaubert and Madame Bovary: A Double Portrait (partial quotation only)
evidence.locator: letter to Madame Tennant, headed Jour de Noël 1876, p. 280

reason: The refutation was right and the line has now failed twice on the same ground: rule 4 requires the translator and year of the published translation whose wording is used, and no named translation prints this English. Worse, the proposed credit is affirmatively wrong. Steegmuller's only located rendering reads ordinary, can and works, so the proposal's orderly, may and work is not his; ordinaire means ordinary, and orderly loses the point the sentence is famous for. Five rival English versions circulate and the one proposed appears solely in quotation books. Crediting Francis Steegmuller 1982 for it would be the confident false citation the standard exists to prevent, and HEDGE cannot waive the translation rule, since the trail runs out on the wording rather than on the attribution. The fit is also thin for a month of stillness and silence: the line is about routine and discipline, not quiet.
